what_its_for: Pacritinib is used to treat a blood disorder called myelofibrosis, which causes scarring in your bone marrow and affects how your body makes blood cells. It is specifically used in adults whose platelet counts are very low (below 50,000 per microliter). It works by blocking certain proteins (JAK2 and IRAK1) that drive the disease, helping to reduce an enlarged spleen and improve symptoms like fatigue, night sweats, and bone pain.
how_to_take: Swallow the capsules whole with a full glass of water. Do not crush, chew, or open the capsules. Take pacritinib with food — having it with a meal can help reduce stomach upset. Try to take your doses at the same times each day to keep a steady level of the medicine in your body. If you vomit after taking a dose, do NOT take an extra dose — just take your next scheduled dose as planned.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 200 mg (two 100 mg capsules) taken TWICE daily, for a total of 400 mg per day. Your doctor may lower your dose if you experience side effects. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — BUT only if your next scheduled dose is more than 12 hours away. If your next dose is coming up in less than 12 hours, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never double up to make up for a missed dose.
storage: Store pacritinib capsules at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep them away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Store in the original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep this medication out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medication down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about a medicine take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit, grapefruit juice, and Seville oranges (often found in marmalades) — they can increase the level of pacritinib in your blood and raise your risk of side effects. Avoid taking certain medications without checking with your doctor first, including blood thinners (like warfarin), antifungals (like ketoconazole or fluconazole), certain antibiotics (like clarithromycin), anti-seizure medications, and herbal supplements like St. John's Wort, as they can interact with pacritinib. Avoid activities that may cause injury or bleeding since this medication can lower your platelet count further. Do not get live vaccines while taking this medicine without talking to your doctor.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience any of the following: unusual or severe bleeding (including blood in urine or stool, coughing up blood, or heavy menstrual bleeding); signs of a blood clot such as sudden chest pain, difficulty breathing, leg pain or swelling; signs of heart rhythm problems like a fast or irregular heartbeat, dizziness, or fainting; severe diarrhea, nausea, or vomiting that does not improve; signs of infection such as fever, chills, or body aches; sudden numbness, weakness, or difficulty speaking (signs of a possible stroke); new or worsening skin symptoms. Also tell your doctor about all medications and supplements you are taking before starting pacritinib.
when_it_works: Most patients start to notice some improvement in symptoms — such as a reduction in spleen size or relief from fatigue and discomfort — within the first few weeks to months of treatment. However, it may take up to 3 to 6 months to see the full benefit. Even if you feel better, continue taking the medication as prescribed unless your doctor tells you to stop.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Pacritinib can harm an unborn baby. Women who could become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 2 weeks after the last dose. Men with female partners who could become pregnant should also use contraception during treatment and for at least 1 week after stopping. Do not breastfeed while taking pacritinib and for at least 1 week after your last dose. Liver problems: If you have moderate or severe liver disease, your doctor may adjust your dose or may not recommend this medication. Kidney problems: No dose adjustment is generally needed for mild to moderate kidney disease, but your doctor will monitor you closely. Older adults (65+): Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects; your doctor will monitor you carefully. Always share your complete medical history with your healthcare team.
